answer: I'd like to talk about a few days I spent deep in the Sundarbans, the huge mangrove forest in the south of Bangladesh. A time I spent immersed in nature that I remember fondly was a three-day boat trip there with a few friends, about two winters ago. We had grown tired of busy streets and craved a proper escape into the wild. From the moment we arrived, the change was [[striking]]; the air was fresh, and the only sounds were birdsong, rustling leaves and the water lapping against the boat. We spent the days gliding along narrow channels, spotting deer, monkeys and even crocodiles on the muddy banks, although sadly no tigers. We slept in small cabins on the boat, and the crew cooked fresh fish for us every evening. Early one morning we walked along a wooden trail through the forest, and the silence was almost eerie. In the evenings we sat on the deck under a sky full of stars. Being so completely disconnected from screens was genuinely [[refreshing]], almost like a reset for my mind, because there was hardly any phone signal. What I found most [[rejuvenating]] was the simple, slow pace of it all. There is something deeply [[grounding]] about being surrounded by nature with none of the usual distractions. Honestly, I returned home feeling calmer and more clear-headed than I had in months. The experience made me realise how much modern life disconnects us from the natural world, and how [[restorative]] it is to reconnect. I would love to go back one day and take my younger sister with me.

followUps.q: Do you often spend time in nature?
followUps.answer: Not as much as I'd like, but I do walk by the Jamuna most evenings. It is not a forest, of course, but watching the river and the open sky helps me unwind after work.

followUps.q: Were you worried about seeing a tiger?
followUps.answer: A little, to be honest, although the guides were very experienced and we mostly stayed on the boat. Part of me was actually disappointed not to catch even a glimpse of one.
